title: How are Foreign Policy Decisions Made in China?
citation: Jakobson, Linda, and Ryan Manuel. 2016. ‘How are Foreign Policy Decisions Made in China?’ Asia & the Pacific Policy Studies 3(1): 101–110.
read_scope: Publisher abstract, introduction including evidence description, and selected body sections; not the complete article.
evidence_method_verified: Introduction describes interviews, case studies, workshops, dialogues, Chinese- and English-language sources, and relationship mapping, drawing on the authors’ prior research.
research_questions: Which formal and informal channels shape mandates and access to leaders?
How do rank and interagency relationships affect coordination?
purpose_and_caveat: Useful bridge into early Xi-era decision making. Its institutional snapshot must be dated, not projected unchanged to 2026 or used to prove instructions in a particular negotiation. Publisher pagination is 101–110; a secondary index gives a conflicting range.

title: China’s Foreign- and Security-policy Decision-making Processes under Hu Jintao
citation: Cabestan, Jean-Pierre. 2009. ‘China’s Foreign- and Security-policy Decision-making Processes under Hu Jintao.’ Journal of Current Chinese Affairs 38(3): 63–97.
read_scope: Original journal abstract, citation and open PDF route checked; article body not read.

access.caveat: Original journal offers a PDF; embedded viewer retrieval failed during screening. That failure does not establish a paywall.

evidence_method_verified: Institutional and historical analysis indicated by the abstract; specific interview or documentary method not verified from the body.
research_questions: What changed in institutional participation and coordination between accession and the Hu period?
purpose_and_caveat: Provides a pre-Xi comparison for centralization and the multiplication of policy actors. A broad account of institutions cannot establish the mechanism behind an individual bargaining pause.

title: China’s foreign and security policy institutions and decision-making under Xi Jinping
citation: Cabestan, Jean-Pierre. 2021. ‘China’s foreign and security policy institutions and decision-making under Xi Jinping.’ The British Journal of Politics and International Relations 23(2): 319–336.
read_scope: Publisher abstract, access label and references; university bibliographic record. Complete body not obtained.

access.request_scope: Complete article, pp. 319–336, including notes and references.
access.caveat: No authorized open full text verified in this search; this does not establish that none exists.

evidence_method_verified: Institutional analysis indicated by the abstract; actual evidence collection must be audited in the full text.
research_questions: Has centralization eliminated fragmentation or altered where it occurs?
How should apparent mandate limits under Xi be tested?
purpose_and_caveat: Abstract argues that coordination and centralization coexist with continuing fragmentation. Compare with Zhao and Taylor–Garlick rather than taking one institutional characterization as settled. Distinguish issue-year 2021 from online-year 2020.

title: Top-Level Design and Enlarged Diplomacy: Foreign and Security Policymaking in Xi Jinping’s China
citation: Zhao, Suisheng. 2023. ‘Top-Level Design and Enlarged Diplomacy: Foreign and Security Policymaking in Xi Jinping’s China.’ Journal of Contemporary China 32(139): 73–86.
read_scope: Search-indexed publisher abstract and issue metadata checked; direct publisher retrieval returned 403. Complete article not obtained.

access.request_scope: Complete article, pp. 73–86, including notes and references.
access.caveat: A failed web fetch is not proof of a paywall. No verified authorized open copy located in this bounded search.

evidence_method_verified: Not verified from body; the abstract describes an institutional explanation of leadership control, coordination and personalized policymaking.
research_questions: What has stronger top-level control changed about delegation and policy flexibility?
purpose_and_caveat: Read alongside Cabestan to identify agreement and disagreement about bureaucratic constraints under Xi. General foreign-policy organization is contextual evidence, not a transcript of a trade negotiation. Issue-year 2023 differs from online-year 2022.

title: ‘Flexible’ versus ‘fragmented’ authoritarianism: evidence from Chinese foreign policy during the Xi Jinping era
citation: Taylor, Monique, and Jeremy Garlick. 2025. ‘“Flexible” versus “fragmented” authoritarianism: evidence from Chinese foreign policy during the Xi Jinping era.’ Australian Journal of International Affairs 79(2): 189–208.
read_scope: Abstract, PDF first-page metadata/license and selected indexed body sections; not the complete article.

access.caveat: Helsinki lists a final published version under CC BY. Direct publisher fetch failed, but institutional availability is verified. Use 2025 issue year, recording 2024 online publication separately.

evidence_method_verified: Read material presents a flexible-authoritarianism argument using foreign-policy case illustrations, including the BRI. Complete case-selection and evidentiary procedures remain to be read.
research_questions: Does variation in implementation indicate fragmentation, or discretion within centrally established objectives?
purpose_and_caveat: A deliberate competing explanation for the fragmentation literature. Test what would demonstrate actual coordination; successful outcomes alone cannot establish a hidden central plan. BRI implementation need not generalize to U.S. negotiation mandates.

title: Authoritarian Audiences, Rhetoric, and Propaganda in International Crises: Evidence from China
citation: Weiss, Jessica Chen, and Allan Dafoe. 2019. ‘Authoritarian Audiences, Rhetoric, and Propaganda in International Crises: Evidence from China.’ International Studies Quarterly 63(4): 963–973.
read_scope: Publisher abstract and 29-page author-manuscript opening checked; not the complete manuscript or final article.

access.caveat: Author copy is dated January 28, 2019, not the final typeset publication. Check version differences before exact citation.

evidence_method_verified: Abstract identifies two survey experiments with Chinese respondents, one using a hypothetical scenario and one reminding respondents of recent events.
research_questions: When do public threats constrain compromise?
Can vague tough rhetoric satisfy domestic audiences without equally specific commitments?
purpose_and_caveat: Relevant to Solomon’s public-sentiment proposition and changes in public diplomacy. Survey approval is not direct evidence of elite instructions or actual concession authority in a crisis.

title: China’s foreign policy rhetoric between orchestration and cacophony
citation: Mokry, Sabine. 2024. ‘China’s foreign policy rhetoric between orchestration and cacophony.’ The Pacific Review 37(2): 360–387.
read_scope: Abstract and selected methods/conclusion sections; not a complete sequential reading.
evidence_method_verified: Qualitative and quantitative content/frame analysis comparing statements by the General Secretary, Premier, State Council Information Office and Foreign Minister, covering 2008–June 2022.
research_questions: Which official actor is speaking, to whom, and how consistently?
purpose_and_caveat: Helps prevent white papers, ministry statements and leaders’ speeches from being pooled into one undifferentiated Chinese voice. Rhetorical divergence does not by itself demonstrate bureaucratic conflict over actual negotiating instructions.

title: What is Lost in Translation? Differences between Chinese Foreign Policy Statements and Their Official English Translations
citation: Mokry, Sabine. 2022. ‘What is Lost in Translation? Differences between Chinese Foreign Policy Statements and Their Official English Translations.’ Foreign Policy Analysis 18(3): orac012.
read_scope: Publisher abstract, conclusion and selected body/footnote passages; not the whole article.
evidence_method_verified: Compares 91 paired Chinese statements and their official English translations, categorizing minor, degree and substantive differences.
research_questions: Do official English translations preserve the force and content of negotiating claims?
purpose_and_caveat: Direct methodological companion to bilingual white-paper and readout work. Translation differences alone do not prove deliberate deception or the translator’s intent; the author identifies motives as a further research question. Partial translations also create selection problems.
